pests.name: Japanese beetles
pests.note_beginner: Shiny metallic-green and copper beetles that show up in summer and chew on the petals and leaves, sometimes skeletonizing them. On a healthy clump the damage is mostly cosmetic. Hand-pick them into soapy water in the early morning when they are sluggish, and avoid the bag-style traps, which pull in more beetles than they catch.
pests.note_seasoned: The classic summer defoliator on coneflowers: adult Japanese beetles feed on ray petals and foliage during the June to August flight, chewing and skeletonizing. Home-scale damage is usually cosmetic on an established plant. Hand-pick into soapy water in the cool of the morning when beetles are sluggish; lure traps tend to draw in more beetles than they remove, so site them far from the planting or skip them.

pests.name: Eriophyid mites
pests.note_beginner: Microscopic mites that live hidden inside the flower buds and cause odd tufted, distorted growth: little green rosettes or leafy bumps sprouting out of the cone instead of a normal flower. There is no easy spray, since the mites are protected inside the bud. Cut off and throw away affected flower heads to reduce them.
pests.note_seasoned: Coneflower rosette mites (Eriophyid mites) are microscopic and live inside developing flower buds, causing tufts of stunted, distorted flower parts and leaf-like growths erupting from the cone. Because they are shielded within the bud, contact miticides are largely ineffective. Management is cultural: prune out and destroy affected heads. This distortion is sometimes confused with aster yellows, but eriophyid damage is localized to individual heads rather than deforming the whole plant.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth, buds, and the backs of leaves and suck sap. They rarely do serious harm. A strong spray of water knocks them off, or use insecticidal soap. Coneflowers also draw in beneficial insects that eat aphids.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth, buds, and leaf undersides; seldom damaging on a vigorous plant and usually held in check by the beneficials coneflowers attract. If populations build on young plants, hose them off or treat with insecticidal soap, per Clemson applied about three times at 5 to 7 day intervals.

pests.name: Rabbits and deer
pests.note_beginner: Rabbits can nibble young coneflower shoots in spring, and while coneflowers are considered fairly deer resistant, hungry deer may still sample them. Established plants usually shrug off light browsing. Protect new plantings with a cage or a repellent if rabbits are a problem in your yard.
pests.note_seasoned: Coneflower is rated deer resistant, but young, tender spring growth can be browsed by rabbits (Clemson notes rabbits can be a real problem) and occasionally by deer under pressure. Established clumps tolerate light browsing. Protect new plantings with fencing or repellents such as hot-pepper wax sprays where rabbit pressure is high.

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.note_beginner: A serious, incurable disease spread by leafhoppers. Infected coneflowers grow strange, deformed flowers: green, leafy tufts or a witches broom that looks like a little broccoli head sprouting from the center, along with stunting and sometimes death. There is no cure and no spray that fixes it. As soon as you see it, dig up and throw away the whole infected plant so it does not spread, and keep down weeds that shelter the leafhoppers.
diseases.note_seasoned: The signature coneflower disease and the one to know: aster yellows is caused by a phytoplasma spread by leafhoppers (and can be carried on tools). Symptoms are diagnostic and bizarre: a witches broom in the flower head that resembles a small broccoli head, greening and deformation of the petals, stunting, and possible death. There is no cure and insecticides do not stop transmission. Rogue out and destroy infected plants promptly (do not compost them), disinfect pruners, and mow or clear weedy, grassy areas that harbor the leafhopper vectors.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A whitish, powdery film on the leaves in warm, humid weather, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It rarely kills the plant but weakens it and looks bad. Space plants for airflow, avoid overhead watering, and remove badly affected leaves. Keeping the plant healthy is the best prevention.
diseases.note_seasoned: A common foliar fungus appearing as a whitish to gray film on leaves, favored by warm, humid conditions and crowded, poorly ventilated plantings. Rarely fatal but it reduces vigor and appearance. Manage culturally: space generously for air circulation, water at the base rather than overhead, remove affected foliage, and maintain overall plant health. Fungicides are available for severe pressure but are seldom needed in the home garden.

diseases.name: Bacterial and fungal leaf spots
diseases.note_beginner: Various leaf spots can appear in wet weather, starting as purplish or brown spots on the lower leaves and moving upward. They usually just spot the foliage and are not fatal. Clean up fallen leaves, water at the base to keep foliage dry, and give plants room to breathe.
diseases.note_seasoned: Bacterial leaf spots (Pseudomonas, Xanthomonas) produce purplish spots that begin on lower leaves and progress upward in wet conditions, per Illinois Extension; fungal spots behave similarly. Mostly cosmetic and rarely fatal. Manage with sanitation (remove fallen debris), base watering to keep foliage dry, and generous spacing for airflow. Bactericides and fungicides are not warranted at home scale for this.

diseases.name: Crown and root rot in wet soil
diseases.note_beginner: The most common way to lose a coneflower is soggy soil. In wet, poorly drained ground the crown and roots rot, the plant wilts and collapses, and it does not come back. This is why coneflowers are often short-lived in heavy or overwatered beds, and why fancy hybrid types fizzle out fastest. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and keep mulch off the crown.
diseases.note_seasoned: Crown, root, and stem rots (including Botrytis and soilborne fungi) are the practical killers of echinacea, driven by wet, poorly drained, or overly rich soil. Symptoms include basal softening, wilt, and collapse; Clemson notes interspecific hybrids in particular may not be reliably hardy in poorly drained soils, which is a chief reason novelty color forms are shorter-lived than the straight species. Management is preventive: excellent drainage, restrained watering, lean rather than rich soil, generous spacing, and keeping mulch pulled back from the crown.
